planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller canopy trees; avoid disturbing the root ball, which resents transplanting once established.

directions: Arnold Pink is a selection made by the Arnold Arboretum from wild mountain silverbell populations, chosen for rose-pink flower buds that open to soft pink, fading toward white as the bell-shaped blooms age. Flowers hang in dense clusters along bare branches in mid-spring ahead of leaf-out, and the tree matures into a broad, loosely pyramidal form that branches low unless limbed up when young. Grow it in humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil in partial shade, siting it as an understory specimen sheltered from strong wind and harsh afternoon sun. Once established it needs little maintenance beyond occasional watering during drought and light corrective pruning to maintain a single leader if a tree form is desired.
sources: Dirr, M.A. Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; stake loosely for the first season to protect the strong central leader.

directions: Introduced by Princeton Nurseries and later recognized with a Theodore Klein Plant Award, Cumulus was selected from Amelanchier laevis for an unusually strong central leader and refined, upright-oval habit that sets it apart from the multi-stemmed clumps typical of the species. Airy clusters of white flowers open in early spring on the bronze-tinged new growth, followed by small blue-black berries that ripen in early summer and draw songbirds quickly. Fall color runs from soft yellow through orange to scarlet, and the foliage shows better resistance to powdery mildew and rust than many seedling-grown serviceberries. Site it in full sun for the densest flowering and best fall color, in moist but well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and expect a tidy, low-maintenance small tree well suited to street tree pits or foundation plantings.
sources: University of Kentucky Nursery Crops Extension

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in average to fertile, moist, well-drained soil; site as a large shrub border specimen or limbed up into small tree form in full sun to open shade.

directions: Cole's Select is a hybrid serviceberry selection valued for glossier, bluish-green summer foliage that turns a richer red-orange in fall than many of its relatives. Clouds of white flowers cover the branches in early spring before the leaves fully expand, followed by sweet, purple-black berries that ripen through early summer for both wildlife and kitchen use. It can be grown as a dense, multi-stemmed large shrub or trained with a single trunk into a small flowering tree, and tolerates open shade as well as full sun. Give it moist but well-drained, moderately acidic soil, and expect minimal pest or disease trouble beyond occasional cedar-apple rust in wet seasons.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; site where hummingbirds visiting the tubular flowers can be observed.

directions: Atrosanguinea is a long-cultivated selection of red buckeye chosen for flower panicles a shade deeper and more saturated than the already vivid scarlet-red of the species, held upright above the palmate foliage in mid-spring. It grows as a large, rounded, clump-forming shrub or small understory tree, dropping its leaves by midsummer in dry sites, a normal trait of the species rather than a sign of distress. Plant it in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade for the lushest foliage, though it also tolerates considerably more sun in cooler climates. The tubular flowers are a magnet for early-migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds, while the glossy brown seeds, like those of the species, are toxic if ingested and should be kept away from small children and livestock.
sources: Dirr, M.A. Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; suitable for foundation plantings where a full-sized buckeye would be too large.

directions: Humilis is a naturally low, spreading form of red buckeye that stays a compact 6 to 8 feet tall and wide, far smaller than the straight species, making it a better fit for shrub borders and smaller gardens. It produces the same narrow, tubular red flowers in erect panicles each spring, though somewhat reduced in size, and remains a strong draw for hummingbirds arriving early in the season. Grow it in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade for the best foliage retention, since red buckeyes of all forms tend to defoliate early in hot, dry summers as a drought-avoidance strategy. The glossy brown seeds are toxic if ingested, so avoid siting it where children or grazing animals have easy access.
